<GuideSummary>
  <Fragment slot="build">
    A tRPC router on the core: guarded procedures, CSRF on every mutation, cookies written only by
    procedures marked to write them, and errors that say no more than the public code.
  </Fragment>
  <Fragment slot="needs">
    [A Node server with Redis and Prisma](/auth/build/node-server/), whose `auth.ts` and
    `config.ts` are used as they are, and `@trpc/server` 11 with `zod` 4.
  </Fragment>
  <Fragment slot="check">
    `router.test.ts` passes: every procedure has an access rule, no query carries a secret, and a
    mutation without the CSRF token is refused with `403`.
  </Fragment>
</GuideSummary>

`@noctcore/auth-trpc` puts the core behind tRPC procedures. The core stays the same: the flows return `AuthResult` values and never throw, and the adapter only decides who gets through, writes the cookies and turns a refusal into a tRPC error that says no more than the public code.

This guide builds on [A Node server with Redis and Prisma](/auth/build/node-server/): `auth.ts` and `config.ts` there are used as they are.

## How the pieces fit

<TrpcWiring />

## Build it

<Steps>

1. ### Install

   ```sh
   bun add @noctcore/auth-trpc @noctcore/auth @trpc/server zod
   ```

   Two of them are peer dependencies, and CI runs the adapter at both floors:

   | Peer           | Range                         |
   | -------------- | ----------------------------- |
   | `@trpc/server` | 11.22.1 or later (within 11) |
   | `zod`          | 4.3 or later (within 4)       |

2. ### The router

   <Code code={routerTs} lang="ts" title="src/router.ts" />

   `createAuthMiddlewares(t)` returns two base procedures and the middlewares behind them. Each refusal carries only its public code:

   | Middleware                 | Lets a call through when                              | Refuses with                                                      |
   | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
   | `publicProcedure`          | a mutation passes CSRF; no session needed             | `forbidden`                                                       |
   | `protectedProcedure`       | it also has a valid session                           | `session_expired`, or `two_factor_enrollment_required`            |
   | `freshAuth(maxAge?)`       | the password proof is newer than `freshAuthAge`       | `fresh_auth_required`                                             |
   | `role(...roles)`           | the user holds one of the roles                       | `forbidden`                                                       |
   | `rateLimited(name, rule?)` | the budget for `name` is not used up                  | `rate_limited`, or `internal` when the counter store does not answer |
   | `writesCookies`            | it is the only cookie writer of an unstreamed mutation | `internal`                                                       |

   - `publicProcedure` checks CSRF on every mutation and needs no session: sign-up, sign-in, the reset request, sign-out.
   - `protectedProcedure` also refuses a caller without a valid session (`UNAUTHORIZED`, `session_expired`) and adds `ctx.user`, loaded from your user store on this request (so a deleted user is signed out at once), and `ctx.session`. Under the two-factor plugin's `enforcement`, a session past the grace window is `enrollment-only`: it is refused (`FORBIDDEN`, `two_factor_enrollment_required`) on every procedure whose meta does not say `twoFactorEnrollment: true`, and so are `freshAuth`, `role` and the nestjs-trpc `AuthGuardMiddleware`, which run the same check. Type the meta with `initTRPC.meta<AuthProcedureMeta>()` to have the key checked. See [Enforcement with a grace period](/auth/build/two-factor/#enforcement-with-a-grace-period).
   - `freshAuth(maxAge?)` asks for a password proof newer than `freshAuthAge`; `maxAge` can only make it shorter. `role(...roles)` reads the roles through the `roles` option of `createAuthContext` on every call, so a role taken away stops working on the next request. Both run the session check themselves.
   - `rateLimited(name, rule?)` counts calls per client IP in a fixed window (10 a minute by default; see [tiers and per-user keys](#rate-limit-tiers-per-user-keys-and-exemptions)), under a key of its own so it never shares a budget with the core's doors. When the counter store does not answer, the call is refused. It does not check CSRF itself: it counts every call that reaches it, in the order of the chain. On `publicProcedure` and `protectedProcedure` the CSRF and session checks run before it, so a forged mutation is refused without using up the victim's budget; on a bare `t.procedure`, or ahead of those checks, it counts forged calls too.
   - `writesCookies` is the only way to the cookie writers. After it, `ctx.auth` has `setSession`, `signOut` and `clearSession`; without it they are not on the type, so an unmarked procedure that calls one does not compile, and from untyped code they throw an `AuthConfigError` before writing anything. Only a mutation may carry it: a query skips the CSRF check and runs on a GET, which a link on another site can send with the `SameSite=Lax` session cookie, so `writesCookies` on a query refuses every call before the procedure runs, as a configuration error (the client sees `internal`). It also refuses a subscription and a streamed batch; see [the client](#the-client).

   `authed`, `freshAuth`, `role`, `publicProcedure` and `writesCookies` each run the CSRF check on a mutation themselves, so leaving the `csrf` step out of a chain does not skip it, and a cookie writer is never reachable from a forged request. The verdict is computed once, when the context is built, so a chain that checks it twice pays only a lookup.

3. ### The context

   <Code code={serverTs} lang="ts" title="src/server.ts" />

   `createAuthContext` checks the options once, and its `node(opts)` (the standalone, Express and nestjs-trpc adapters) or `fetch(opts)` builds `ctx.auth` once per HTTP request, so every procedure of a batch shares it:

   - the session cookie is read and validated through the core (`validateRequest`); a token the core refused for good is cleared (`clearsSessionCookie`), one another request may still be adopting from your own store is kept;
   - the client IP comes from the core's `clientIp`, counting `trustedHops` from the right of `X-Forwarded-For` (at most 16), or skipping the proxies a `trustedHops` list names by address (CIDR ranges and the presets `loopback`, `linklocal` and `uniquelocal`); with `clientIpHeader` set (such as `cf-connecting-ip`, off by default), a single-address header from your edge wins, but only with `trustedHops` as a proxy list (a hop count is refused at boot), only when the socket address is inside it, and only when it holds exactly one IP. The list must name the edge, or hops that accept traffic only from it (see [Trust proxy and client IPs](/auth/learn/trust-proxy-and-client-ips/));
   - the three CSRF checks are computed from the headers: the `Origin` is on the allowlist, `Sec-Fetch-Site` says `same-origin` when the browser sends it (or `cross-site` from an origin on `csrf.crossSiteOrigins`, for a desktop shell; see [Cookies and desktop shells](/auth/learn/cookies-and-desktop-shells/)), and the double-submit token matches its cookie and is bound to this session or pre-session;
   - on a query, the page gets what it needs for its next mutation: a pre-session id when it has none, and a CSRF cookie bound to the current session or pre-session. Both take the `SameSite` that `session.cookie.sameSite` gives the request's `Origin`, like the session cookie.

   The CSRF cookie is readable by the page, which echoes it in the `x-csrf-token` header on every mutation; see [the client](#the-client).

   A failure while building the context (a store down) answers `internal`, and only the error's name is logged: a store error can carry the session key.

   The WebSocket adapter (`applyWSSHandler`) is not supported yet. It builds the context once per connection and passes the socket as `res`, so the cookies a first visit needs could not be set, and a session would be validated once and kept after a sign-out, a password change or a revocation until the socket closed. `node(opts)` refuses a `res` that cannot set headers with an `AuthConfigError` before it reads anything: the client sees `internal` and the connection is closed.

   The Fastify adapter is not supported yet either. A Fastify reply has `getHeader` but no `setHeader` (that is on `reply.raw`), so `node(opts)` refuses it the same way, on every request.

   #### On the fetch adapter

   <Code code={fetchTs} lang="ts" title="src/fetch.ts" />

   A fetch `Request` carries no peer address, so pass it from your server (on Bun, `server.requestIP(req)?.address`). Behind proxies, count them in `trustedHops` as on Node (without a peer address the count picks the same `X-Forwarded-For` entry it would with one), or list them by address: with a list and no peer address, nothing is trusted.

   #### Background polls

   Every request that carries a session counts as activity and refreshes its last-active time, at most once per `touchInterval`. For procedures the page calls on its own, such as a poll on a timer, mark them passive so an idle session still expires while only they are called (see [Background polls](/auth/learn/sessions-and-expiry/#background-polls)): set `touch: false` in the procedure's meta, or pass `createAuthContext` a `touch` predicate over procedure paths, such as `touch: (path) => path !== 'notifications.count'`. Both are read from the calls tRPC parsed before it built the context, and a batch touches when any of its procedures is active. A passive call is still answered with its session, and the CSRF verdict and the guarded procedures do not change. `touch: false` on `createAuthContext` touches on no request; the default touches on every one.

   Three cases where the option or the meta has no effect:

   - **nestjs-trpc with `AuthModule` mounted.** The session is validated twice, and each validation decides on its own whether to touch: first the Nest `CsrfMiddleware` (on every route), with `AuthModule`'s `touch` option, then the tRPC context, with `createAuthContext`'s `touch` and the procedure meta. The last-active time is written when either says touch, so a poll stays passive only when it is marked in both: in `AuthModule`'s predicate (the path it sees is the HTTP path, such as `/trpc/notifications.count`, where a batch joins its procedures in one path with commas) and by `meta({ touch: false })` or the `createAuthContext` predicate. If `/trpc` is in `csrf.exempt`, the middleware returns before it validates, and the tRPC side is the only switch (see [Use with NestJS](/auth/build/nestjs/#background-polls)).
   - **The WebSocket adapter.** It is not supported yet, and `node(opts)` refuses its connections (see [The context](#the-context)). On `@trpc/server` 11.28.0, the version checked, it builds the context once per connection and names no call, so the option and the meta could not apply to a subscription on it.
   - **A predicate that returns a promise.** The result is compared with `false` only, so an async predicate always touches.

   The meta flag is read from tRPC's `call.procedure`, which tRPC marks `@internal`; the meta test in `packages/auth-trpc/tests/background-polls.test.ts` fails if a tRPC upgrade drops the field.

   #### Subscriptions

   tRPC builds the context once per HTTP request, and a subscription served over SSE (`httpSubscriptionLink`, on by default in `@trpc/server` 11) is one request that stays open until the client leaves or `sse.maxDurationMs` ends it, which has no default. The session is validated when the stream opens, so on its own a stream opened before a sign-out, a password change or a revocation would go on sending events to that browser. A reconnect is a new request, validated like any other.

   So every session check (`authed`, `freshAuth`, `role`, `protectedProcedure`, and the nestjs-trpc `AuthGuardMiddleware`, `AuthedMiddleware`, `FreshAuthMiddleware` and `RoleMiddleware`) keeps a subscription's events behind it. Before an event leaves, when the last check started longer ago than the `revalidateSubscriptions` option of `createAuthContext` (default `'30s'`; a number means seconds), the session is validated again and its user loaded. When either is gone, or the session became enrollment-only, the stream ends with `session_expired` (or `two_factor_enrollment_required`) in place of the event: tRPC sends it as the stream's error event and `httpSubscriptionLink` closes the subscription without retrying. The procedure's own iterator is returned, so its `finally` runs as it does when the client leaves.

   The server example above sets `revalidateSubscriptions: '30s'`, the default.

   - **The bound.** An event is not sent once the last check that saw the session live started longer ago than `revalidateSubscriptions`. A check counts from when it started, so a revocation that lands while a check is reading the store is caught by the next one. The bound is read on the core's clock (the wall clock by default), which is not monotonic: a clock stepped backwards delays the next check by the step. `0` checks before every event; `false` turns the check off and the stream keeps the session it opened with.
   - **The cost.** One session validation and one user read per open stream per bound, and only while events flow: a stream that sends nothing reads nothing, and its connection stays open until its next event, the client leaving, or `sse.maxDurationMs`. Set `sse.maxDurationMs` in `initTRPC.create({ sse: { maxDurationMs } })` too if idle streams should not stay open for long.
   - **No touch.** The check does not count as activity, so an open stream never keeps an idle session alive, whatever `touch` says. A page that only reads a stream sends no activity, so once `idleTimeout` passes the stream ends with `session_expired` and the user is signed out, as on any idle page.
   - **A store failure.** It ends the stream with `internal`, logging only the error's name. `internal` is a code `httpSubscriptionLink` retries, so the client reconnects, and the new request is validated like any other; `session_expired` and `two_factor_enrollment_required` close the subscription without a retry.
   - **What is checked again.** The session, its user and the enrollment-only standing. A role and a fresh proof are checked when the stream opens, and not again until the client reconnects. A public subscription has no session check, so one that reads `ctx.auth.session` keeps the session it opened with: build it on `protectedProcedure`.
   - **Observables.** A procedure that returns an observable is read as an async iterable, as tRPC's SSE handler reads it.

4. ### The client

   <Code code={clientTs} lang="ts" title="src/client.ts" />

   `httpBatchStreamLink` (the create-t3-app default) sends the response headers before any procedure of the batch runs, so a cookie set by a procedure cannot reach the browser: on the fetch adapter it would be dropped, on Node the write would fail after the flow had already run. The adapter does not let either happen silently:

   - `writesCookies` refuses the call on a streamed batch before the procedure runs, so no sign-in, rotation or sign-out happens without its cookie. The client sees `internal`, and the server gets an `AuthConfigError` naming the fix. It decides what is streamed exactly as tRPC does: the `trpc-accept` header when present, otherwise an `Accept` header that lists `application/jsonl`.
   - A subscription's response is a stream too, so `writesCookies` on a subscription refuses every call, as a configuration error. Write cookies from a mutation (a query is refused too; see [the router](#the-router)).
   - A procedure without `writesCookies` has no writers at all (see [the router](#the-router)), so it cannot reach this case.

   So route mutations to `httpLink` or `httpBatchLink`, with `splitLink` as above. Queries can keep streaming: the pre-session and CSRF cookies are written when the context is built, before the stream starts.

</Steps>

## Cookies on sign-in and rotation

Every flow that issues a session hands it to `ctx.auth.setSession(issued)`, in a procedure marked `writesCookies`, which writes the session cookie, the trusted-device cookie and a CSRF cookie bound to the new session, and returns the token for the response. That covers sign-in and every rotation: `reauthenticate`, `changePassword`, `sessions.revokeOthers` and the email verification flows. A token from before the rotation stops verifying the moment the new cookie lands. `ctx.auth.signOut()` signs out through the core and starts a fresh pre-session; after `sessions.revokeAll`, pass its blank cookie to `ctx.auth.clearSession(cookie)`.

<Aside type="caution" title="One procedure per HTTP request writes cookies">
  If two session-writing procedures shared a batch (two sign-ins, or a sign-in and a rotation),
  both flows would run, the browser would keep only the cookie written last, and the other session
  would stay valid with no browser holding it. Send session-writing mutations one per request, as
  [the client](#the-client) does.
</Aside>

So the first procedure of a batch to reach `writesCookies` claims the request, and any other marked procedure in the same batch is refused before it runs: the client sees `internal`, and the server gets an `AuthConfigError`. Which one wins depends on timing, not on its place in the batch. As a backstop, a second `setSession`, `signOut` or `clearSession` call in one request throws before writing. Procedures without the marker share a batch freely.

## Rate limit tiers, per-user keys and exemptions

`createAuthMiddlewares(t, { rateLimits })` takes named rules, checked when the middlewares are made (a bad name, a `limit` that is not a whole number of at least 1, a `window` that is not a duration longer than zero, or a bad `keyBy` throws an `AuthConfigError` at boot, and so does the same in a rule passed to `rateLimited`):

```ts
const t = initTRPC.context<Context>().meta<RateLimitMeta>().create({ errorFormatter: authErrorFormatter });

const { publicProcedure, protectedProcedure, rateLimited, writesCookies } = createAuthMiddlewares(t, {
  rateLimits: {
    default: { limit: 20, window: '1m' },
    sensitive: { limit: 5, window: '1h', keyBy: 'user' },
  },
});

exportData: protectedProcedure.use(rateLimited('export', 'sensitive')).mutation(/* ... */),
logout: publicProcedure.use(writesCookies).meta({ rateLimit: 'exempt' }).mutation(/* ... */),
```

- **Which rule.** `rateLimited(name, rule)` counts with `rule` when given: a tier name (typed from the keys of `rateLimits`, and an unknown one throws at boot) or a rule of its own. Without one it takes the tier named `name`, else the tier named `default`, else 10 a minute. The budget belongs to `name`: two procedures that pass the same name share one budget, two names never do, whatever tier they use.
- **Who is counted.** By default, the client IP. A rule with `keyBy: 'user'` counts a signed-in caller by user, so a user keeps one budget across IPs and users behind one shared IP (an office, a carrier NAT) stop spending each other's. The user comes only from the session the core accepted, never from anything the client sent: a call with no session, or with a cookie the core refused, counts by its client IP, so a made-up cookie is no fresh budget. The counter key holds the core's keyed hash of the user id (an HMAC under a key derived from the server secret, like session handles), so a reader of the counter store cannot link a key to a guessable user id.
- **Exemptions.** A procedure whose meta says `rateLimit: 'exempt'` is never counted, including by a `rateLimited` on the base procedure it was built from, so a sign-out cannot be rate limited out. Add `RateLimitMeta` to your meta type (`initTRPC.meta<RateLimitMeta>()`, or extend it); `AuthProcedureMeta` already includes it. Meta is set in your code, never by the client.

<Aside type="caution" title="Two traps">
  Per-user keys give each account its own budget, so someone with many accounts has many budgets:
  on a procedure anyone can call, keep a per-IP limit too. And meta set on a base procedure carries
  to every procedure built from it, so `rateLimit: 'exempt'` on a shared base exempts all of them:
  put it only on the procedure that needs it.
</Aside>

## Verification links

`verifyEmailLink` in the router is a mutation on `publicProcedure`, so it is a POST and checks CSRF. The context resolves the session on public procedures too: pass `ctx.auth.session` as it is (`null` when nobody is signed in). A link for one account opened while signed in as another is then refused (`session_expired`) and stays usable for its owner. By default a link opened with no session is refused the same way; with `emailVerification.linkWithoutSession` on it verifies the address and signs nobody in.

<Aside type="caution" title="Never verify on page load">
  Never verify from a query or when the page loads: mail scanners fetch links in mail, and with
  `linkWithoutSession` on a fetch that reaches the flow verifies the account. Put the token in the
  URL fragment (``urls.verifyEmail: (token) => `${origin}/verify#${token}` ``), show a Confirm
  button, and call the mutation on the click. See [Email
  verification](/auth/learn/email-verification/) for the trade-off.
</Aside>

## Errors

Throw `toTRPCError(result)` when a flow refuses. The message is the public code, there is no cause, and the tRPC code follows a fixed table (`AUTH_ERROR_TRPC_CODES`): `invalid_credentials` is `UNAUTHORIZED`, `rate_limited` is `TOO_MANY_REQUESTS`, `fresh_auth_required` and `forbidden` are `FORBIDDEN`, and so on. A code the table does not know becomes `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` with the message `internal`, never the raw value.

`authErrorFormatter` adds `data.auth` (the public code and, on `rate_limited`, `retryAfterSeconds`) and covers what tRPC builds itself:

- no error carries a stack, in development or production (tRPC adds one whenever `NODE_ENV` is not `production`, with absolute paths);
- an input that fails validation is answered with the message `invalid_input` and `data.input`, a list of paths and issue codes, never the submitted value;
- any other `BAD_REQUEST`, such as a body that is not JSON (the parser's message quotes the body), and the request errors `PARSE_ERROR`, `METHOD_NOT_SUPPORTED`, `UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE`, `PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE` and `NOT_FOUND` (tRPC's quotes the requested path) are answered with a fixed message, the code in lower case, whoever raised them;
- any internal error is answered with `internal`, without its message.

<Aside type="caution" title="Your own errors keep their message">
  An error your own procedure throws with any other code (`CONFLICT`, `FORBIDDEN`) keeps the message
  you gave it, so keep secrets and account state out of it.
</Aside>

Sign-in answers an unknown email and a wrong password with the same error, and sign-up and the reset request answer a taken and a new address with the same `{ status: 'accepted' }`, as long as your procedure returns the same thing in both cases, as the router above does.

## Schemas

The package exports a Zod input and output for every auth flow. The outputs are plain objects that strip every key they do not name: `userOutput` sends `id`, `email` and `emailVerified`, whatever your user record grows. Declare `output:` on every procedure that returns a record.

`inspectPasswordResetInput` (`{ token }`) and `resetInspectionOutput` (`{ userId, email, expiresAt, secondFactorRequired }`) are for a reset page that checks its link on load with `auth.inspectPasswordReset`. The token is a secret: put the procedure on a mutation.

`sessionListOutput` names each session by its public `handle`, never its store key, and strips a store key a procedure returns by mistake. `revokeSessionInput` takes that handle (`{ handle }`); see [Session handles](/auth/learn/sessions-and-expiry/#session-handles) for what revoke answers.

The inputs check shape and size only; whether an email is valid or a password long enough is the flow's answer, with its public code. Every input that carries a secret belongs to a mutation, since tRPC sends a query's input in the URL, where access logs, proxies and browser history keep it.

## nestjs-trpc

The same middleware bodies come as classes for nestjs-trpc. Register `AuthGuardMiddleware` in `globalMiddlewares`: it checks CSRF on every mutation and requires a session on every procedure unless its meta says `auth: 'public'` (`@Mutation({ meta: { auth: 'public' } })`), so a procedure nobody marked is closed. `WritesCookiesMiddleware` (with `@UseMiddlewares`) is the only way to the cookie writers, as on plain tRPC: without it, `setSession`, `signOut` and `clearSession` throw an `AuthConfigError` before writing anything. nestjs-trpc types `@Ctx()` by hand, so type it as `{ auth: AuthWriter }` only on marked procedures; the compiler cannot check the marker there. `signOut` refuses before the core signs out, but in an unmarked procedure `setSession` refuses only after your flow ran (a rotation then leaves the browser without its new session), so mark every procedure that issues a session. `RoleMiddleware(...roles)`, `FreshAuthMiddleware(maxAge?)` and `RateLimitMiddleware(name, rule?)` make the classes (a rule may say `keyBy: 'user'`; a tier is a rule constant passed to each class that uses it, and `@Mutation({ meta: { rateLimit: 'exempt' } })` skips the count) for `@UseMiddlewares(...)`, once, at module level; list every class in a module's `providers`. A role or fresh-proof class on a procedure marked public refuses every call, as a configuration error, and so does `WritesCookiesMiddleware` on a `@Query` or a `@Subscription`: put it on a `@Mutation`.

The context class returns `authContext.node(opts)`, and the error formatter goes in `trpc: { errorFormatter: authErrorFormatter }`.

## Check it works

The test runs the same flows over in-memory stores, so it needs no Redis or Postgres. The site runs this file with `node --test`.

| Test                                                             | Passes when                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| every procedure has an access rule, and no query carries a secret | `assertProceduresGuarded` and `assertNoSecretQueries` find nothing in the router                             |
| a mutation without the CSRF token is refused, and passes with it  | `register` answers `403` with the cookies alone, and `200` once the `csrf` cookie is echoed in `x-csrf-token` |

<Code code={routerTestTs} lang="ts" title="src/router.test.ts" />

- `assertProceduresGuarded(router)` fails on a procedure built on `t.procedure` with neither `publicProcedure` nor a session check, on one built on `publicProcedure` that also asks for a session, a role or a fresh proof (the two say opposite things), and on a query or subscription marked `writesCookies`, which the middleware would refuse on every call. It checks which markers a procedure carries, not their order: a `rateLimited` placed ahead of the session check passes it.
- `assertNoSecretQueries(router)` fails on a query or subscription whose input has a key naming a secret (`password`, `pwd`, `token`, `code`, `secret`, `otp`, `hotp`, `pin`). It splits a key into words (camelCase, snake_case, kebab-case) in one linear pass, so `currentPassword` and `reset_token` match, and it matches plurals (`recoveryCodes`, `apiTokens`) and run-together lower-case names ending in a secret word (`resettoken`, `accesstokens`, `otpcode`, `verificationcode`, `pincode`, `newpin`, `2facode`). `credential`, `jwt`, `bearer` and `authorization` match as the last word only (`credentials`, `accessJwt`), so `credentialId`, `jwtIssuer` and `authorizationUrl` pass. Key pairs match written as two words or one: `apiKey`, `privateKey`, `accessKey`, `signingKey` and `encryptionKey`, while `publicKey` and a bare `key` pass. Names that only look like a secret word (`postcode`, `barcode`, `pinned`, `spinner`, `keyboard`) pass, and `sessionId`, `pass` and `signature` stay out on purpose: each is as often a plain identifier, a flag or a value meant for a URL. A postal `pincode` field is flagged like `pinCode` always was; allow its path once checked. It walks every part of a Zod 4 schema: object shapes and catch-alls, array elements, tuple items and rest, record, map and set keys and values (a record keyed by an enum or literal is checked by its values), unions, intersections, both sides of a pipe, and wrapped and lazy schemas. It fails closed on what it cannot read: `z.preprocess()` (its function sees the raw input before any schema), a validator that is not Zod 4, `z.unknown()` and `z.any()` (a loose object's catch-all among them), `z.custom()` and `z.instanceof()`, and any Zod type it does not know. It also fails on a lazy router. List a path in `allow` once you have checked it by hand. A record keyed by `z.string()` accepts any key name, which no static check can see.

Both walk a plain tRPC router. They cannot see into nestjs-trpc, which builds its router at boot. Neither can see what a procedure's handler calls, so they cannot report a cookie writer without `writesCookies`; the type of `ctx.auth` does that at compile time instead, and the writers refuse at run time.
